To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a tonalitic–granitic–trondjemitic (TTG) layer can evolve in the upper mantle by fractional crystallization of tholeiitic magmas, 2) the TTG layer will be stably buoyant, 3) it will crystallize from the top downwards, 4) its thickness will be several kilometres, and 5) its crystallization will be accompanied by convection in the underlying mantle and in the overlying crust,

(i) the Archean crust formed from a tonalite magma layer, which was generated by the partial melting of a thick, hot mantle; (ii) this tonalite layer was a shallow magma ocean, which formed by open-system fractional crystallisation; and (iii) the tectonic consequences are that the Archean continent was a thick, stable and buoyant layer of tonalitic rocks that formed by a process of convection.
The Archean crust formed by the crystallization of a global tholeiitic layer that formed at shallow levels in the mantle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the petrology and tectonic implications of the evolution and tectonics of a tonalite magma ocean within Archean cratons.
the following topics: the evolution of the early continental crust, the evolution of the continental crust in general, the origin of the continental crust, and the origin of the early Earth.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Archean TTG crust was produced by the crystallization from a shallow, tholeiitic, open-system magma ocean, and that this crystallization was largely from the top downward, but that the crystallization from the bottom up was possible in some areas of extremely low heat flow.

the evolution and tectonics of the continental crust are not controlled by a deep, hot mantle plume or asthenosphere, but by a shallow, cool mantle plume or lithosphere, the latter of which is a much smaller-scale convective cell.

the evolution and tectonics of early continents is controlled by a tonalitic–granitic magma layer which evolves by localized open-system fractionation of an almost global, shallow-level tholeitic magma ocean.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a tonalitic–granitic magma layer in the upper part of an Archean continent, produced by open-system fractional crystallisation of a shallow tholeiitic melt, could have been stable for long periods.
the Archean continents formed in a very different way than those of the Proterozoic and Phanerozoic.
the evolution of a tonalite-trondhjemite-granodiorite (TTG) layer within the Archean lithosphere has a profound influence on tectonic patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of a mantle plume, a tonalite magma layer can form and remain stable in the uppermost mantle.
, while the Archean crust was dominated by TTG rocks and the Archean mantle was dominated by MORB-like magmatism, the two were not necessarily in the same places.
a shallow, tholeiitic, tonalitic–granodiorite magma layer, formed by fractional crystallization of a global tholeiitic basalt layer, is a viable model for the early Archean crust.
